headline: A Harvard Business School online course that lets students pitch start-up ideas to AI versions of its professors has led an Indian academic to ask whether AI teachers could help fill India's classroom gaps.
score_reason: Pool 4 lowered by 1: an opinion column whose Harvard facts are second-hand from the New York Times and undated, with no new decision or result.
importance_line: What changed is that a leading business school is selling teaching delivered partly by AI copies of its professors, which matters first to students and teachers, then to universities, but this is one academic's opinion built on a second-hand New York Times report, not research or a policy step.
source: Scroll.in, citing The New York Times
summary: Scroll.in carries a commentary by Angshuman Kar, a professor of English at The University of Burdwan, on Harvard Business School's eight-week online bootcamp HBS Foundry, which costs $699 and lets participants pitch start-up ideas to AI avatars modelled on real professors, details Kar takes from a New York Times report. Kar's view, not a reported finding, is that such avatars could ease India's shortage of maths and science teachers, but that they may also widen an "AI divide" between students with and without internet, devices and English, and cannot replace the trust a human teacher builds.
notes: Full text read on the AMP page of Scroll.in. It is a signed opinion column; the Harvard details rest on a New York Times report that the column does not date or link, so the Harvard launch date is unknown. Printed link is the AMP page we read.
